chapter.title: Rationale
chapter.para: The largest of those removals is the range of supported targets. The 2006 RexxHTTP was portable along three axes at once: it ran under both CGI and mod_rexx, on OS/2 and Windows as well as Unix, and targeted Microsoft IIS beside Apache. Much of the original rationale was the bookkeeping of holding those axes together: reconciling the variables CGI provided with the ones mod_rexx provided, working around an OS/2 Object Rexx that lacked a MutableBuffer, and so on. The 1.0 keeps one point in that space: CGI, on Apache, on a current &Rexx;. mod_rexx is no longer maintained upstream, and IIS and OS/2 are not current targets. Committing to a single gateway is what allows the rest of the design to stay simple. Several of the decisions below began as compromises between two gateways. With one gateway left, each reduces to a single answer, and the sections below state that answer rather than the negotiation behind it.

The wider original design is described in full by the manual that shipped with it: Josep Maria Blasco, RexxHttp: Servlet programming in Rexx, version 0.1, 2 November 2006, available at https://www.epbcn.com/pdf/josep-maria-blasco/2006-11-02-RexxHttp-Servlet-programming-in-Rexx.pdf. That manual remains the record of the portable, multi-gateway design. The present manual documents the narrower 1.0 that grew out of it, and the decisions below are the ones that narrowing settled.

section.title: Associating Rexx Files with a Handler
section.para: A rexxlet is an ordinary &Rexx; file, and the web server has to be told to run it through RexxHTTP rather than serve it or execute it directly. Apache's Action directive is the mechanism: it binds a handler name to the RexxHTTP processor, and Apache invokes the processor for the rexxlet files that fall under that handler. The 2006 manual described the same approach. It asks nothing unusual of Apache, because Action is a stock directive and the routing is data in the configuration rather than logic in the processor.

What has changed is the recommended default. In 2006, broad extensions (.htm, .html, .rsp) were mapped to the handler, because the aim was to run whole trees of pages, some of them compiled, through one gateway. The 1.0 has no page compilers and no such aim. The chapter recommends the opposite default: a whitelist, so that only the files explicitly marked are run as rexxlets and everything else is served as a static file. On infrastructure that has served tens of thousands of URLs for years, running as code only what is named is the conservative default. Opening an extension to the handler is the exception, and is made deliberately.

section.title: The Environment-Variable Request Model
section.para: CGI delivers a request as a set of environment variables, and RexxHTTP takes that literally: the request object answers any message it does not recognise with the value of the like-named environment variable. &Rexx; programs reach their world through Value and through variables. Resolving request~remote_addr to the REMOTE_ADDR the server set means a rexxlet author reaches the CGI environment the same way as everything else, without a lookup table or an import step. The mechanics are in the Class Reference under .

This raises one question. If request~anything can name an environment variable, then a variable can share a name with a method, present or future, and the author needs a predictable answer to which one wins. The 2006 manual settled it by carving out a namespace: operator-set variables had to begin with an underscore, where no method would ever live. That rule required the author to remember a naming convention, and the variables that motivated it (timezone hints for the old Netscape-style cookies, settings for the page compilers) are gone from the 1.0. The rule went with them, in favour of two forms of access instead of one reserved name. request~name is the library's view, where a method wins when one exists, exactly as &Rexx; method lookup already works. request["name"] is the raw variable underneath, which always reaches the environment pool and never a method. An operator-set variable is then an ordinary variable, requiring no underscore: SetEnv MYAPP_MODE production is request~myapp_mode. If a future method ever shadowed it, the bracket form would still reach it. The collision question is answered by giving the author access to either side of a name, not by reserving names.

section.title: The Problem of Request Values
section.para: The 2006 rationale gave the title the problem of request values to a real difficulty: what Apache invokes is the RexxHTTP processor, not the rexxlet, so the raw CGI variables describe the processor's invocation rather than the request the rexxlet means to read. The CGI specification is also ambiguous or self-contradictory in places, and the 2006 system had to reconcile what CGI reported with what mod_rexx reported for the same notion.

With mod_rexx gone, the second half of that problem no longer arises: there is one gateway, so there is nothing to reconcile. What remains is the first half, reconstructing the values a rexxlet should see from the values the processor is handed. The 2006 design made a commitment here that the 1.0 keeps: where CGI is inconsistent, RexxHTTP is consistent, and it documents what its methods mean rather than passing the server's quirks through. Three cases from the original still describe how the methods behave:

path_translated always answers the full filesystem path of the document being served, whether or not there is extra path information after it. The CGI specification's definition of this variable is incoherent: it promises a translated version of the extra path info, which by construction has no physical mapping. Apache, left to itself, returns a value of no use here. RexxHTTP answers the useful meaning and holds to it. Where the client names a rexxlet directly the document and the processor are one file; where an Action routes the request they are two, and script_filename names the processor.

script_name always answers the virtual path that locates the rexxlet, with any extra path information stripped, which is what building self-referential URLs requires. path_info answers that extra path, decoded, or the null string when there is none. The split between the two is deliberate, so that a rexxlet can ask where it is and what followed it as separate questions.

request_uri (with its alias unparseduri) answers the request URI exactly as the client sent it, still encoded. uri answers the decoded path with the query string removed. Naming both, with stable meanings, removes any need to determine which encoding and which trimming a given server applied.
All three follow the same principle: the request object is a specification a rexxlet can rely on, not a pass-through of what the gateway reported.

section.title: Strict by Default
section.para: The 1.0 parses GET and POST arguments under a single, default, and currently only argument policy, strict. Every parameter must be a genuine name=value pair, the name must be a usable &Rexx; symbol, and the name must be unique caselessly. A request that breaks any of these is answered 400 Bad Request before the rexxlet runs at all. The mechanics are in . The decision is to make this the default rather than an opt-in.

The reasoning is specific to the kind of service RexxHTTP exists to run. For a public site with a large, stable set of URLs, which is the case RexxHTTP was extracted from, malformed argument input cannot have come from the site's own pages, and the predictable response is to reject it before the rexxlet runs. Strict-by-default turns a class of ambiguous input into a 400. In exchange, every rexxlet downstream can assume that each argument it sees has a name and a value, and that a name names exactly one argument. The check is made once, at the boundary, so that no rexxlet has to repeat it.
